# Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta (MN 52 (PTS MN i 349))

**ID:** MN 52 (PTS MN i 349)  
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta  
**PTS:** MN i 349  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul0.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul0.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The eleven doors expounded by Ānanda consist of the four form-sphere jhānas, the four divine abodes (*cattāro brahmavihārā*), and the first three formless attainments, stopping short of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception [Hung 2010; Wen 2011; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. In Ānanda's instructions, each attainment serves as an object of insight: the practitioner enters the state and actively reflects that it is conditioned, volitionally produced, impermanent, and subject to cessation [Hung 2010; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Shulman 2014]. Established in that reflection (*tattha*), the meditator either destroys the mental cankers (*āsavakkhaya*) to achieve arahantship or, if any fetters linger, eliminates the five lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) to become a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) [Hung 2010; Schmithausen 1981; Wen 2011]. In the commentary (*Papañcasūdanī*), Buddhaghosa glosses *tattha* as referring to that unified state of *samatha* and *vipassanā*, emphasizing the integration of concentration and insight into impermanence [Saitanaporn 2009].

The discourse has a direct Pali parallel in AN 11.16 (the *Dasama Sutta*), with closely related treatments of meditative insight appearing in AN 9.36 and MN 64 (*Mahāmālukya Sutta*) [Hung 2010; Schmithausen 1981]. Curated non-Pali parallels include two Chinese translations: MĀ 217 in the *Madhyama Āgama* and the individual translation T 92 (*Shizhi jushi bacheng ren jing*), as well as citations in the *Abhidharmasaṅgītiparyāyapāda* (T 1537.15) [Schmithausen 1981; Wen 2011].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: AN 11.16 Aṭṭhakanāgarasutta; MA 217 八城; T 92 十支居士八城人
- Passage-level parallels: MN 64 (PTS MN i 432) Mahāmālukya Sutta; AN 9.36 Jhānasutta; T 1537.15 覺支品

**Sources**

- [Saitanaporn 2009] Phramonchai Saitanaporn, Buddhist Deliverance: A Re-evaluation of the Relationship Between Samatha and Vipassana (2009) — Buddhaghosa's commentary in the Papañcasūdanī glossing 'tattha' as samatha and vipassanā.
- [Hung 2010] Ya-Chun Hung (Bhikkhuni Syinchen), Issues in Samatha and Vipasyana: Comparative Study of Buddhist Meditation (2010) — Identification of Dasama as interlocutor, the formula of conditioned and impermanent nature of the eleven states, and parallel to AN Dasama Sutta.
- [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995] Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Middle Length Discourses of the Buddha (1995) — Sutta title translation and analysis of jhānas, immaterial attainments, and divine abodes as objects of insight.
- [Rogell 2003] Sharda Rogell, Pressing Out Pure Honey: A Practitioner’s Study Guide (2003) — Dasama's opening inquiry regarding a single quality for mental liberation.
- [Shulman 2014] Eviatar Shulman, Rethinking the Buddha: Early Buddhist Philosophy as Meditative Perception (2014) — Contemplation of meditative attainments as impermanent, conditioned, and leading to cessation.
- [Schmithausen 1981] Lambert Schmithausen, 'Liberating Insight and Enlightenment' (1981) — Attainment of arahantship or destruction of lower fetters (anāgāmitā) across the states, and comparative remarks on Chinese parallels.
- [Wen 2011] Tzungkuen Wen, A Study of Sukkhavipassaka in Pali Buddhism — Enumeration of the eleven attainments (four jhānas, four brahmavihāras, three formless jhānas) leading to third or fourth stage of enlightenment; mention of MĀ 217.
